/uk-news/2026/sep/24/police-arrest-far-r.headline: Police arrest far-right activist Daniel Thomas two days after Channel dinghy was slashed
/uk-news/2026/sep/24/police-arrest-far-r.bodyHtml:
Police have arrested Daniel Thomas, the far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist, on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life, two days after he filmed himself slashing the side of a dinghy in the middle of the Channel while a rescuer was on board.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said a 37-year-old man, of no fixed abode, was arrested on Wednesday night “on suspicion of destroying ships or fixed platforms or endangering their safety under section 11 of the Aviation and Maritime Security Act 1990”.

Officers said Thomas was suspected of “criminal damage, criminal damage with intent to endanger life, and conduct endangering ships, structures or individuals under section 58 of the Merchant Shipping Act 1995”.

Thomas appears to have filmed his own arrest on Wednesday night. A video uploaded to his YouTube channel shows the arrest, apparently at a garage, with an officer telling him he had been “involved in criminal damage that has recklessly endangered someone’s life”.

Thomas, who prefers to go by the name Danny Tommo, replied: “I understand. I knew this was coming.”

Over the summer Thomas has brought dozens of nationalist protest groups together under the umbrella movement Patriot Platform.

He organised this month’s anti-immigration marches by masked men in Dover and Portsmouth.

/us-news/2026/sep/24/judge-orders-trump-.headline: Judge restores White House access for CNN, MS Now and Politico
/us-news/2026/sep/24/judge-orders-trump-.bodyHtml:
Journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico are to return to the White House after a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to temporarily restore their access, saying the president’s ban on the three outlets was likely unconstitutional.

US district judge Tim Kelly issued the order in a lawsuit the news organisations filed contesting the ban that the president announced on 18 September.

Kelly ordered the administration to return the outlets’ press passes immediately and issued a temporary restraining order that will be in effect for 14 days. Such orders are typically designed to preserve the status quo while the court reviews the case more closely.

Earlier on Wednesday Kelly cited past case law that clearly laid out the need for a distinct process, with advance notice of an infraction and an opportunity to plead one’s case.

Prior cases made clear, the judge said, that “before a journalist’s White House hard pass was suspended or revoked, that the journalist was entitled to pre-deprivation notice and an opportunity to be heard”.

A justice department lawyer told the judge the administration had given a sufficient explanation for revoking the press passes in letters sent to the outlets on Tuesday. The judge signalled scepticism, noting that the letters were sent after the revocation had happened and the lawsuit had been filed.

Trump had said on social media that the three outlets “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES”, and justice department lawyers had sought to justify the ban on national security grounds.

The three outlets sued Trump and other members of his administration in federal court in Washington on Monday, arguing the ban violated the US constitution’s first amendment protections for free speech and a free press, as well as their due process rights. They asked for a temporary restraining order to reinstate their White House access immediately while their legal challenge plays out.

In a legal filing on Tuesday, the justice department argued that access to the White House is a privilege, not an entitlement, and that the president has the authority to suspend access by news organisations.

The outlets did not stand alone. A coalition of press freedom groups and dozens of news organisations filed a legal brief on Wednesday in their support, asserting that “stripping journalists and news outlets of their rights because of perceived editorial viewpoint violates decades of supreme court jurisprudence”.

The brief was signed by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, Reuters, the Washington Post and Fox News, among others.

/society/2026/sep/23/approach-to-high-bl.headline: Better blood pressure detection could prevent tens of thousands of heart attacks and strokes, experts say
/society/2026/sep/23/approach-to-high-bl.bodyHtml:
The largest study of its kind has mapped the scale of high blood pressure in England, finding that millions of people are unaware they have the “silent killer” condition and that only half of those treated by a GP have it under control, a picture that researchers say makes the case for population-wide prevention.

Most people with hypertension (59%) are undiagnosed, according to the study, and therefore at raised risk of stroke, heart attack and early death, risks that fall once the condition is found and brought under control.

Even among those diagnosed and receiving medication through their family doctor, blood pressure is uncontrolled in 50% of cases, the Oxford University study of 1.4 million adults suggests.

Researchers said the findings, published in the journal BMJ Public Health, showed the current approach to detecting and treating high blood pressure in England was “not fit for purpose”.

The study used data from the Our Future Health programme and looked at people enrolled between 2022 and 2025 with high blood pressure, defined as 140/90 mmHg or higher.

Researchers calculated that more than a third of adults (37%) had high blood pressure, with six in 10 of these unaware of their condition.

Hypertension was almost 50% more common in men than women (42% compared with 29% across all ages), and more common in older people, according to the research.

Detection and control of high blood pressure improved substantially during the 2000s, the researchers said, before progress plateaued from about 2011.

There were also “indications of worsening trends following the Covid-19 pandemic, possibly because disruptions to healthcare delivery may have had lasting effects”.

Wenyu Liu, a medical statistician at Oxford Population Health and lead author of the study, said: “While hypertension is largely a ‘silent killer’, the current approach to detecting and treating high blood pressure is not fit for purpose.

“Our study highlights the prevalence of hypertension across demographics. This underscores the need for population-wide prevention strategies alongside targeted treatment for people at high cardiovascular risk.”

The researchers said “the most striking finding” was the high absolute number and proportion of people with undiagnosed hypertension, alongside the finding that only half of adults treated by a GP were adequately controlled.

Dr Iain Turnbull, a GP, deputy chief medical officer at Our Future Health and a clinical research fellow at Oxford Population Health, said it was not yet clear why 50% of patients who reported taking blood pressure-lowering drugs had uncontrolled hypertension, and set out the range of possible reasons.

“Blood pressure varies considerably between people, and some people need changes in dose or two or more different medicines before it is brought under control. Other health conditions and medications can affect blood pressure, too.

“There are also practical and social factors: side effects, complicated treatment regimens and competing health or life pressures can make medicines difficult to take consistently. Weight, diet, salt intake, alcohol and physical activity can also influence blood pressure.

“So a high reading can have many explanations and shouldn’t be seen simply as a reflection of what an individual patient or healthcare professional has done.

“There are also some important caveats … we did not have prescribing records available to independently confirm medication use, and a blood pressure measurement on one day does not necessarily represent someone’s usual blood pressure.

“Even with those caveats, I wouldn’t regard 50% as a satisfactory figure. Persistently high blood pressure increases the risk of stroke and heart disease, and bringing it under control reduces that risk.”

Prof Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer at the British Heart Foundation, said the study “paints a concerning picture of the scale of undetected high blood pressure in the UK, and the challenges of keeping blood pressure under control in those already receiving treatment”.

“Better detection and treatment could help tens of thousands of people to avoid a preventable heart attack and stroke,” he added. “But to achieve this, we will need to rethink how we identify, treat and support those at risk so that blood pressure checks and effective treatment can benefit everyone.”

/environment/2026/sep/23/uk-climate-cris.headline: UK takes climate security findings to foreign ministers as Miliband announces taskforce and £330m for nature
/environment/2026/sep/23/uk-climate-cris.bodyHtml:
The UK has taken the findings of a climate and national security report suppressed under Keir Starmer to foreign ministries around the world, warning them that the climate and nature crises and the coming El Niño threaten their security and defence, and setting out how it intends to respond.

Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, made a presentation to the foreign ministers of the EU as well as Kenya and other countries on Wednesday night at a private meeting during the UN general assembly in New York, based on the report by the UK’s spy chiefs that found the collapse of natural systems around the world would lead to conflict, migration and food shortages.

Miliband told the meeting, the first such discussion among foreign ministers, that the coming El Niño, supercharged by climate breakdown, would test the world’s food systems as never before.

“We face an El Niño that is already set to be the most intense in living memory,” he said. “This will intensify climate shocks that compound and cascade across borders, threatening food and water security, displacing communities, putting pressure on markets and scarring economies.”

This year’s heatwaves, bad harvests and food price inflation had shown governments what they were in for, he said, and the response must come from the highest levels.

“Climate change and nature loss have never been issues for climate and environment ministers alone,” he said. “They are defining challenges for our citizens, our economies, our foreign policy and our national security.”

With the backing of Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, Miliband presented the research, which found that the collapse of global ecosystems such as the Amazon and Congo rainforests, driven by the climate crisis and the destruction of nature, would have impacts on national security around the world.

The joint intelligence committee (JIC) report, revealed by the Guardian, had been scheduled for publication last October but was suppressed on the eve of its launch by Downing Street. A redacted version was issued in January under the Freedom of Information Act; ministers have so far resisted calls for the full report to be made public.

Richard Nugee, a retired general and security expert, told the Guardian governments must treat the climate as they would other threats to national security, such as sabotage by hostile states.

“If a bridge is washed away, it has the same impact whether it’s done by [a foreign power] or the climate,” he said. “The climate crisis will affect food security, energy security, water security, and lead to migration and potentially the recruitment of farmers to [terrorist organisations such as] Isis. Countries should absolutely be treating this as a national security issue.”

He said it was not surprising that the JIC report had been suppressed and redacted, as it was “very rare” for security reports to be published.

Miliband will appoint a new special representative for climate security, and a new ministerial taskforce on “the national security and resilience risks of a changing climate and nature loss”, bringing military and security experts together with climate scientists.

He also announced £330m for the Global Environment Facility, the main international fund for protecting nature, to go towards protecting forests, oceans and other critical ecosystems in developing countries.

The closed-door meeting was convened after Miliband made a public speech on Monday at the UN general assembly on the links between the climate and national security. Soon after taking office in July, the former energy secretary told the Guardian he would put the climate at the heart of UK foreign policy.

On Wednesday night, Miliband said: “The countries fit for the future will be those that see climate and nature as intrinsic to economic and national security. Countries that anticipate risks and invest in resilience before crises hit.

“Countries that seize the incredible opportunities the clean energy transition presents. Countries that don’t just see the connections but act on them.”

He added: “That is why the UK is placing climate and nature security at the heart of our national security and foreign policy decision-making.”

Adrian Ramsay, the Green party MP for Waveney Valley, who has campaigned for the JIC report to be made public, said: “It’s good that the foreign secretary is presenting the findings of this crucial report to ministers from other governments.

“But it begs the question, why are MPs in this country still being denied access to the full report? And, most importantly, why has our government still not published its response to how it will address the stark findings?”

/world/2026/sep/24/netanyahu-to-deliver-.headline: Netanyahu heads to UN to make Israel’s case as protesters and allies press for change
/world/2026/sep/24/netanyahu-to-deliver-.bodyHtml:
When he takes the stage at the UN on Thursday, Benjamin Netanyahu will deliver a familiar message of defiance, even as protests and international condemnation leave the Israeli leader increasingly isolated and allies press him, through diplomacy and sanctions, to change course.

Netanyahu is facing his toughest re-election challenge in a political career spanning decades, with three ongoing conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, and a growing campaign of violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank. Israeli voters will have their say in October.

Internationally, Israel faces growing condemnation, and allies are turning it into action: the UK, France and Canada are planning to sanction Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and the British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has accused Israeli settlers of committing ethnic cleansing of Palestinian communities.

In the US, public opinion is in the midst of a historic shift: 62% of respondents told Pew in July they had a negative opinion of Netanyahu’s government, and 60% of American Jews in a poll released this week said they hoped he would be voted out in October.

Protests are expected both in the UN’s general assembly hall and on the streets of New York City, where the mayor, Zohran Mamdani, has tempered his earlier promises to arrest Netanyahu as a war criminal and assured demonstrators this week that he would protect their “right to [protest] in this city”.

Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, defended Netanyahu’s government in a telephone interview before the speech, seeking to cast criticism of Israel’s actions as the product of misinformation and bias.

“We are aware of the fact that we had a very challenging three years since October 7,” said Danon. “We accomplished a lot, but we were criticised. We were under the spotlight, and for us, I think, we are proud of our achievements.”

“At the same time, we will work harder to improve the image of Israel, and we know there’s a campaign against us,” he added.

Anger at Netanyahu will be on full display in New York City on Thursday, where several protests have been scheduled, including a march from Bryant Park in midtown Manhattan to the UN headquarters in Turtle Bay to “reject war criminal Benjamin Netanyahu and the genocidal Zionist project”.

“Netanyahu is coming to New York amid a political environment that has made it crystal clear that he is not welcome here,” said Beth Miller, the political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action.

She described a “mainstreaming” of public opinion that “Americans do not want to be supporting Israel’s genocide. We do not want to be supporting Israel’s apartheid. We do not want to be arming Israel or supporting Israel.”

Palestinian representatives are calling for diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech to “send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end”.

In Danon’s telling, Israel’s problem was largely one of public relations rather than policy, and he cited a “wave of misinformation” as the reason for the precipitous shift in polling. Netanyahu would use his speech to “highlight Israel’s achievements”, he said, and to lay out “what still should be done, and how should we verify that we actually achieve the goals of the war?”

He did not elaborate on those measures before the speech, but the White House and US policymakers will be listening as they calibrate their message to voters, and weigh the backlash of public anger, ahead of the midterm elections.

Netanyahu is expected to deliver a hardline message aimed not just at world leaders but at his own electorate ahead of the October elections. “I think that he is trying to demonstrate to the Israeli populace that he still maintains some level of control over the situation,” said Miller. “And I think that he is trying to speak to a rightwing audience and a Trump-Maga audience in this country to try to rile up the hatred and Islamophobia.”

Donald Trump and top US officials are not expected to meet Netanyahu during a visit expected to last less than 24 hours. Trump will be in Washington DC hosting the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, and Netanyahu has cited Israel’s election campaign and the holiday of Sukkot as his reasons for heading home quickly after the speech.

A Trump administration official said Netanyahu’s delegation had sought a high-level meeting during the visit but none was organised. There are also no plans to meet congressional leaders, Danon said.

With criticism from top Republicans, including the vice-president, JD Vance, and leading Democratic presidential contenders, Israel could face a 2028 campaign in which neither candidate supports arms sales to Israel or the broad diplomatic backing it has enjoyed in the past.

Even within the Maga base there are fractures, Miller noted, with “more and more people who don’t really want to be sending our tax dollars to support the Israeli government”.

Danon said of a potential shift in the US-Israeli security relationship: “I think that we are still sharing the same values, and that’s why I’m sure that we will continue to have the support from the US.”

There are multiple flashpoints for anger from both US political parties and the international community, including dire humanitarian concerns and the lack of reconstruction in Gaza, the expansion of settlements in the West Bank, and continued conflicts in Lebanon and Iran, where the US has found itself mired in a conflict that has driven up global energy prices.

Asked if a controversial $2.8bn (£2.1bn) arms sale indicated that Israel was preparing to resume its offensive in Gaza, Danon said Israel “hopes that we will see [Hamas’s] disarmament without our involvement”, nodding to efforts by the Trump-backed Board of Peace. If that does not change, he said, Israel “will do it ourselves”, adding: “We can not leave it forever like that.”

He was equally resolute on the West Bank, saying Israel would not be swayed by recent criticism led by the UK over plans to expand settlements including E1, the planned construction that would sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank.

Senate Democrats are introducing a bill on Wednesday to sanction facilitators of the new settlement. Senator Chris Coons, a co-sponsor, said in a statement that “as Palestinian civilians face a campaign of devastation and fear from violent extremist settlers, the United States must send a strong message that this behaviour is unacceptable”.

The protests began even before Netanyahu arrived in New York.

On Wednesday, several members of the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York City chapter rallied at John F Kennedy international airport in protest at weapons and explosive materials destined for the Israeli military being flown out of the airport on commercial aircraft.

Aber Kawas, who in November is set to become the first Palestinian-American elected official in New York state, spoke at the event and later told the Guardian she plans to join many other New Yorkers protesting against Netanyahu’s UN speech on Thursday.

“Thousands of people are against his presence in our city,” she said.

Some had hailed Netanyahu’s decision to cut his visit short as a victory, she added, but “the fact that he is coming shows he continues to have a sense of entitlement to be centred on the world stage while being the head architect of a genocide”.

/us-news/2026/sep/23/trump-xi-jinping-ch.headline: Trump greets Xi Jinping on the tarmac as US and China extend trade truce
/us-news/2026/sep/23/trump-xi-jinping-ch.bodyHtml:
Donald Trump has welcomed Xi Jinping to the US with an unusual personal greeting on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews, opening a state visit to Washington on the same day the two countries agreed to extend their trade truce.

Xi’s plane was met with a lavish arrival ceremony that included a 30-metre-long (100ft) red carpet flanked by US service members, a military flyover by two B-1 bombers and a presentation of the flags and national anthems of both countries.

US presidents typically welcome foreign leaders at the White House, but Trump and the first lady, Melania Trump, travelled to the military base in Maryland, just outside Washington, to personally shake hands with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, on their arrival on Wednesday evening.

Xi’s visit comes as world leaders gather in New York for the United Nations general assembly, although the Chinese leader will not address the meeting. He has attended the UNGA just once since becoming president in 2012.

“It’s pretty notable that Xi Jinping is coming to Washington in the same week as the general assembly, but does not feel bothered to come up to New York,” Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group told Reuters.

“I think a lot of people will say, ‘Where is the real center of decision-making?’”

The visit began with progress on trade. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, announced that the US and China had agreed on Wednesday to extend the so-called “Busan agreement”, a temporary truce between the world’s two biggest economies.

Bessent, who met the Chinese vice-premier, He Lifeng, earlier on Wednesday, told Fox News the agreement would be extended until 10 January, two months beyond its original expiry.

The pageantry will continue with a formal state welcome on the South Lawn of the White House, private tea with the US president and first lady, and a tour of the National Archives, among other special events.

The trade dispute is one of many thorny issues Trump and Xi will confront over the two-day visit, along with the race in artificial intelligence and geopolitical instability.

On Thursday, the White House has invited major tech leaders, including executives from OpenAI, Apple, xAI, Microsoft, Nvidia and Meta, to a state dinner being held for Xi.

There was one discordant note in the carefully orchestrated ceremony: Trump visibly winced at the sound of a US military jet flying overhead as he stood alongside Xi on the red carpet during the US national anthem. Video of the moment showed Trump recoiling from the flyover while Xi, and the wives of both men, remained impassive.

The moment, widely mocked online, was captured on a White House livestream but left out of the edited highlights of the ceremony released by Trump’s aides later.

The US and China have long competed to develop increasingly powerful technology, and the race to advance AI has become a major topic among tech companies, especially after several executives came forward to warn about the dangers of rapid development.

Trump has dismissed concerns that AI development could harm people, instead promoting more investment in the technology so that the US can beat China in the race.

“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last week.

The president and members of the administration have insisted that leading AI development also means leading the world militarily and economically, raising the stakes further for both countries.

Xi’s visit is expected to be filled with ceremonial displays, reciprocating the treatment Trump received when he visited China earlier this year.

Trump’s decision to greet the Chinese leader at his plane, rather than at the White House, shows how far the US president is willing to go to honour Xi.

“He’s coming on our soil,” Melania Trump told Fox & Friends on Wednesday morning, “and we need to welcome them with the most respect.”

Robert Mackey contributed reporting

/australia-news/2026/sep/24/anthony-alba.bodyHtml:
Anthony Albanese has confronted OpenAI over an artificial intelligence agent that hacked Medicare in June, after the tech giant notified the government earlier this month by way of an email to a “public mailbox”.

Australia’s prime minister made the comments at the UN summit in New York, saying it appeared no personal information had been accessed in the breach.

Investigations assisted by the Australian Signals Directorate are under way into how the agent infiltrated Australia’s government-run universal healthcare system and three other services.

They were the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the Victorian Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia.

“This situation is obviously unacceptable,” Albanese said.

“Today, I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident and I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred.”

Albanese said both the delay and the manner in which OpenAI notified the government were disappointing.

“It took until 10 September before there was any notification at all. And the notification was an email sent to just the public mailbox,” Albanese said.

The email was sent to the public-facing address publicdisclosures@servicesaustralia.gov.au. That inbox is checked once a day, and the email was not read until 11 September.

Services Australia then reported the notification to the Australian Cyber Security Centre on 15 September.

A taskforce has been launched to examine the “legal situation” of the breach.

The NSW premier, Chris Minns, and the Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, both said on Thursday that Albanese had informed them the OpenAI breach had touched state websites: NSW’s crime agency and Victoria’s health department.

Minns and Carroll said it did not appear any personal information had been shared, though investigations were ongoing.

“New South Wales will be working with commonwealth intelligence agencies to get to the bottom of it,” Minns said.

How the hack happened

Albanese said the OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access to the public-facing Medicare statistics reporting service portal, which is administered by Services Australia.

The portal contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics, such as spending.

Albanese said the agent had accessed “public and non-public files within the portal” and, in order to do so, had “engaged in writing files as well to the internal server”.

The deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, said the government had learned of the June breach “a couple of weeks ago” and ministers were informed last week.

Marles said the agent was non-human and called the breach a “very serious incident”.

“What we have seen is unauthorised access in to an Australian government website and that is completely unacceptable and we have made that clear to OpenAI,” he said.

The AI agent had been given “a benign task” of researching health and medical statistics and, in doing so, had approached the three other Australian websites as well as the Medicare portal.

“In relation to those three, it interacted in a way that a member of the public might, so it only acted in an authorised way,” Marles told ABC radio on Thursday.

“But in relation to the medical portal of Services Australia, it sought information, information was not given, and then it effectively hacked into that medical portal and got that information anyway.

“It’s that unauthorised access which we are very concerned about. The impact is relatively minor, but the incident is very serious.”

‘Legal situation’ under investigation

Marles said the government had established a taskforce led by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, working with the Australian Signals Directorate and the AI Safety Institute.

“We will look at what is the legal situation in respect of this and what it means to have gained an unauthorised access, albeit in an unintended way,” the acting prime minister said.

“This is a warning about the fact that artificial intelligence, which is a technology that has huge opportunity to benefit humanity, has to be developed with enormous care. There have to be guardrails and safety measures in place which are way ahead of the capability which is being developed.”

The OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company was conducting an extensive review of “misaligned model activity during training and evaluation” and was “notifying third parties when our review identifies potential impacts to their systems”.

“During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation,” Pusateri said in a statement.

“In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend.”

He said the review had found aggregate health statistics and internal file names had been accessed but there was “no evidence of patient records being accessed”.

Pusateri said OpenAI was supporting the investigations and that its review was ongoing, adding that it was committed to “sharing what we learn as that work continues”.

Australians should be ‘worried’

Lizzie O’Shea, spokesperson for Digital Rights Watch, said the three months it took OpenAI to tell the government showed the need for “basic rules and standards for tech companies”.

“Artificial intelligence has potential to do some things well, but it also poses huge risks – like hacking systems that store Australians’ sensitive personal data,” O’Shea said on Thursday.

“The question is whether governments are going to let AI and tech companies run wild or whether they, on behalf of ordinary people, will put rules in place for tech companies that will promote accountability and trust.”

The independent senator David Pocock said the OpenAI hack highlighted how slow the government had been to implement AI safeguards in high-risk settings.

Pocock criticised the government’s decision to shelve plans for a National AI Safety Act, and its dilatory approach to legislating new standards.

“We have these companies warning of existential threat and hacking critical government infrastructure and the Labor government’s response is ‘We’ll get to that next year’.

“There is also a big question here around why we aren’t holding these big tech companies liable for this kind of data breach. If it was an Australian who hacked the system they’d likely be heading for jail, yet there’s no accountability for AI companies developing this technology.”

Ed Santo, former human rights commissioner and co-founder of the Human Technology Institute, told ABC radio that Australians ought to “be worried”.

“This is the first time that this has happened in any major way to an Australian database, and it’s one of the most sensitive databases that we have in government.”

OpenAI had “instructed their AI agents to go looking for information about the public health system in Australia. When the AI agents couldn’t easily find that information, they decided to break the law,” Santo said.

Describing the behaviour as “misaligned model activity” was using “a very euphemistic term”, he said.

“If we were in the bricks and mortar world, if an employee of a company went and broke the law, particularly if it broke the criminal law, then that individual would suffer serious legal consequences, but so would their company. And so we need to make sure that that is true also in this era of AI.”

/artanddesign/2026/sep/24/greek-pm-deal-.headline: Parthenon marbles deal still within reach with ‘political will and courage’, says Greek PM
/artanddesign/2026/sep/24/greek-pm-deal-.bodyHtml:
The Greek prime minister has said a deal to return the Parthenon marbles can still be reached with “political will”, setting out what an agreement could bring to both countries, though Greece will not accept a loan in the style of the Bayeux tapestry’s visit from France.

Writing for the Guardian, Kyriakos Mitsotakis said Greece “cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum’s ownership of the sculptures, or a scheme that would mean we ‘borrow’ parts of our own monument”.

He made the intervention weeks after the British Museum director, Nicholas Cullinan, told the Financial Times that France’s 10-month loan of the Bayeux tapestry to the British Museum could provide a model for a deal. The director said there was “no cookie-cutter template” but the exchange was an example of a successful international partnership.

In his article, Mitsotakis says the situation with the Parthenon marbles is completely different, as half of the frieze is in Athens, and no one would suggest cutting the Bayeux tapestry in two.

Pointing out that Andy Burnham once backed returning the marbles, the Greek prime minister said “political will and courage” would be needed, and that Greece would accept nothing less than “reunification” of the marbles in Athens.

Reunification, he said, could become “the foundation of a broad and enduring cultural partnership between our countries, creating new opportunities for exhibitions, scholarship, conservation and exchanges between Greek and British museums”, which was “the prize”.

It comes amid speculation about the status of talks between the British Museum and the Greek government over the return of the antiquities, with the Telegraph reporting they were on the brink of collapse.

Sources close to the talks disputed that characterisation, while acknowledging there was a large gap to bridge in the long-running dialogue.

Burnham, who once said the marbles should be given back to Greece, has said more recently that it is a matter for the British Museum.

The Parthenon marbles are also known as the Elgin marbles after the British peer Lord Elgin, who removed them from Athens more than 200 years ago.

Carved 2,500 years ago by Phidias, a master sculptor, the antiquities embellished the Parthenon’s monumental frieze before their removal in highly contentious circumstances by Elgin, who was Britain’s ambassador to the Ottoman empire. Bankrupted by his endeavours, Elgin then sold them to the British government in 1816.

It has been a decades-long cultural dispute between the UK, whose law prevents the British Museum from returning items from its collection, and Greece, which considers the objects to have been plundered.

George Osborne, the former chancellor and current chair of the British Museum, confirmed in 2023 that he was in talks with Greece about a deal, while also saying he was not attempting to change the law, a reference to the British Museum Act 1963, which prohibits the museum from permanently removing objects from its collection.

At the time, it was proposed the arrangement could involve the sculptures being in London and Athens at different times, with Britain receiving “Greek treasures” in return.

The British Museum said its position, and its openness to a deal, was unchanged.
